edition.deck: A historic summit in Shenzhen, renewed Gulf attacks and major UK policy disputes lead this evening’s news.
edition.editorialNote: Prioritises consequential developments and fresh reporting. Returning subjects are included only where the gather adds a distinct update or useful new angle.

content.headline: Trump, Putin and Xi prepare for historic three-way talks in China
content.shortHeadline: Trump, Putin and Xi prepare for historic talks
content.standfirst: The leaders have met ahead of Thursday’s first in-person trilateral meeting. Ukraine may be discussed, but the agenda is not public and Kyiv and European leaders will not be at the table.

image.caption: Vladimir Putin is back on the global stage as he prepares for talks with Donald Trump and Xi Jinping.

sources.originalTitle: Trump shakes hands with Putin and Xi ahead of historic talks in China
Steve Rosenberg: Historic talks with Xi and Trump are a coup for Putin
As Trump and Xi meet, China's AI dreams face an unexpected hurdle: the Nvidia spy scandal

segments.body: Donald Trump and Vladimir Putin greeted one another in Shenzhen on Wednesday, as the US president arrived for an Asia-Pacific summit hosted by Xi Jinping. The three leaders are due to hold talks together on Thursday, the first time they have met as a trio.

segments.title: Ukraine and the summit’s symbolism
segments.body: The full agenda has not been published. Possible subjects include Ukraine, Iran, nuclear proliferation, trade and AI. Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky has voiced concern that a plan to end the war could be discussed without Ukraine or Europe present; it remains unclear whether Beijing wants the war on the agenda.

perspectives.body: The BBC’s Steve Rosenberg argues that the meeting’s imagery is already a diplomatic gain for Putin, who can present himself as a global statesman. He cautions that the optics do not mean Russia is closer to winning the war.

segments.body: The summit also comes amid tension over advanced chips. US intelligence claims about an alleged Chinese spy and Nvidia’s former chief remain unproven; Beijing calls them a smear. The allegations have revived debate in Washington about restricting chip exports to China.

content.headline: Kuwait and Bahrain report Iranian attacks after US strike on Qeshm
content.shortHeadline: Iranian attacks reported after US strike on Qeshm
content.standfirst: The renewed exchanges raise fears of escalation in a nine-month conflict, while a tanker attack in the Strait of Hormuz left one crew member missing, according to the vessel’s operator.

sources.originalTitle: Kuwait says it repelled first Iranian attack in two months after US strikes island

segments.body: Kuwait and Bahrain say their air defences intercepted Iranian attacks overnight. Iran’s military said it targeted an airbase in Kuwait that hosts US forces; Kuwait reported no damage. The attacks followed a US strike on a missile launch site on Iran’s Qeshm Island.

segments.title: Tensions on the water
segments.body: Abu Dhabi National Oil Company said a search was under way for a missing crew member after one of its tankers was attacked in the Gulf. The UK Maritime Trade Operations centre reported a tanker struck by an unknown projectile near Oman; Iran said ships had caught fire after hitting mines. The accounts do not establish who was responsible for the tanker incident.

content.headline: AI helps uncover a critical security flaw in widely used Java software
content.shortHeadline: AI uncovers critical flaw in widely used Java software
content.standfirst: The vulnerability could let an attacker run unwanted commands in Java’s memory system. Oracle has issued a security update, but it is not yet known whether any organisations were affected.

sources.originalTitle: Security flaw found in Java, world's third-largest programming language

segments.body: Cybersecurity firm Calif says it used OpenAI’s GPT-6 Cyber model to find a serious vulnerability in Java, the programming language used across sectors including banking, aviation and government. The flaw could allow an attacker to run unwanted commands in a system’s memory.

segments.title: A patch, but unanswered questions
segments.body: Oracle issued a critical security update that includes fixes for the flaw. It is not yet clear whether any companies or platforms were affected. Researchers say the discovery adds to concerns about long-standing software vulnerabilities, while also showing how AI can help security teams find and fix them.

content.headline: Canada looks to Chinese carmakers as US tariffs pressure its auto industry
content.shortHeadline: Canada weighs Chinese investment amid US auto tariffs
content.standfirst: Mark Carney says Canada will pursue its options as tariffs weigh on carmakers and jobs. Chinese investment could offer a route forward, but no vehicle deal has been announced and the idea faces political resistance.

sources.originalTitle: Canada weighs Chinese investment as US tariffs threaten its auto industry

segments.body: Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney says the United States’ concerns about Canada’s ties with China are not a top issue for Donald Trump. The two leaders discussed trade in a brief meeting on the sidelines of the APEC summit, while Canada considers whether Chinese carmakers could help sustain its auto industry.

segments.title: Investment and political risks
segments.body: US tariffs have contributed to job losses in Canada, where most cars made are sold to the US. Carney has said Chinese investment could create Canadian manufacturing jobs, but the countries have not announced a vehicle agreement. US officials have warned Ottawa against closer ties with Beijing, while critics in Canada question the impact on local jobs and the wider North American industry.

content.headline: US loses measles-free status as UK lawmakers warn of falling vaccination rates
content.shortHeadline: US loses measles-free status as UK vaccine rates fall
content.standfirst: The US, Bolivia and Mexico have lost official verification after sustained measles transmission. In a separate warning, a UK Lords committee says falling childhood vaccination coverage puts public health gains at risk.

sources.originalTitle: Why the US has joined the UK on a warning list for a deadly disease

segments.body: The Pan American Health Organization says the US, Bolivia and Mexico have lost verification as free from endemic measles after sustained transmission. The US has recorded more than 4,000 cases this year, according to the report, which cites gaps in immunity, barriers to healthcare, misinformation and vaccine hesitancy among contributing factors.

segments.title: A warning from UK lawmakers
segments.body: A UK House of Lords committee says pre-school vaccination rates in England have fallen for more than a decade and are now below the World Health Organization’s standard. Coverage of the first MMR dose fell from almost 93% around 2013 to below 88% in 2025–26. The committee says lower coverage and widening inequalities put preventable illness and death at risk.

content.headline: Democrats nominate Hakeem Jeffries for US House Speaker
content.shortHeadline: Democrats nominate Hakeem Jeffries for Speaker
content.standfirst: The party’s House members backed Jeffries in a 251–11 vote. If elected when the new Congress convenes on 3 January, he would be the first Black lawmaker to lead the chamber.

sources.originalTitle: Democrats nominate Hakeem Jeffries to be US Speaker of the House

segments.body: Democrats have nominated Hakeem Jeffries to be Speaker of the US House of Representatives after a 251–11 vote. His election is widely expected when the House chooses its Speaker on 3 January, when Democrats are due to hold a majority.

Seven incoming lawmakers, including members of the party’s left wing, said there was still work to do to ensure the party’s direction reflects what constituents want. Jeffries has led House Democrats since 2023.

content.headline: Anthropic founders poised for multibillion-dollar stakes as shares go on sale
content.shortHeadline: Anthropic founders face multibillion-dollar windfall
content.standfirst: The AI company behind Claude is preparing to sell shares on the US stock market. At the top of its proposed price range, each founder’s stake would be worth at least $18.5bn on paper.

image.caption: Anthropic co-founders Dario and Daniela Amodei.

source.credit: David Paul Morris/Bloomberg via Getty Images

sources.originalTitle: The seven Anthropic founders who are about to become multi-billionaires

segments.body: Anthropic, the company behind Claude, is preparing to float its business on the US stock market at between $70 and $78 a share. If shares sell at the top of that range, the seven founders’ holdings would each be worth at least $18.5bn, according to the report.

segments.title: From OpenAI to Anthropic
segments.body: The founders left OpenAI in 2021 to establish Anthropic, which has grown rapidly in five years. Chief executive Dario Amodei and his sister Daniela, the company’s president, led the departure; the other founders have roles spanning research, engineering, policy and AI safety.

content.headline: Lucy Letby trial expert had been barred from treating patients, report finds
content.shortHeadline: Letby trial expert had been barred from treating patients
content.standfirst: A Guardian investigation says a hospital excluded Professor Peter Hindmarsh from clinical practice over patient-safety concerns during Letby’s trial. The prosecution and defence were not told of that decision, raising questions about disclosure.

image.caption: Professor Peter Hindmarsh, whose evidence featured in Lucy Letby’s trial.

sources.originalTitle: Doctor whose evidence helped to convict Lucy Letby was barred from treating patients during trial

segments.body: University College London Hospitals trust barred paediatric endocrinologist Peter Hindmarsh from treating patients in March 2023, while Lucy Letby’s trial was still under way, according to documents seen by the Guardian. Hindmarsh had given evidence for the prosecution about insulin poisoning; the jury was not told of the hospital’s safety concerns or its decision.

segments.title: Disclosure and the conviction
segments.body: The Guardian reports that the Crown Prosecution Service says it was not told of the later restriction or a tribunal ruling that year, and therefore did not disclose them to the defence. Letby’s lawyer says Hindmarsh’s evidence was central to the case and has applied to the Criminal Cases Review Commission. The report raises questions about the evidence and disclosure; it does not establish that Letby’s convictions are unsafe.

content.headline: UK inflation rises to 3.6% as petrol prices reach a four-year high
content.shortHeadline: UK inflation rises to 3.6% as fuel prices climb
content.standfirst: October’s rise was driven in part by higher fuel prices, with diesel reaching its highest level in records dating to 1996. Forecasters expect further pressure on household bills and borrowing costs.

image.caption: Fuel prices rose sharply in October, pushing up the cost of motoring.

sources.originalTitle: UK inflation rises to 3.6% after petrol and diesel prices hit record high

segments.body: UK inflation rose from 3.5% in September to 3.6% in October, the highest rate in a year, according to the Office for National Statistics. Petrol cost 174.7p a litre on average, its highest price in four years; diesel reached 199.5p, a record in data dating back to 1996.

segments.title: Bills and interest rates
segments.body: The figures include a 4% increase in the energy price cap from October. Cornwall Insight forecasts a 26% rise in Great Britain’s energy bills from January, while the Bank of England expects inflation to climb further next year and says higher interest rates may be needed. Food-price inflation eased to 0.9%, its slowest rate since September 2021.

content.headline: NHS report finds years of unnecessary chemotherapy harmed brain tumour patients
content.shortHeadline: Report finds unnecessary chemotherapy harmed NHS patients
content.standfirst: A review of 20 cases at an NHS trust found 15 involved unsatisfactory care, including prolonged treatment without evidence of benefit. The trust has apologised and says it is taking action.

image.caption: University Hospital Coventry, part of the trust reviewed in the report.

sources.originalTitle: Cancer patients at NHS trust harmed by years of unnecessary chemotherapy, report finds

segments.body: A Royal College of Physicians report found that patients with brain tumours at University Hospitals Coventry and Warwickshire NHS trust received years of chemotherapy without evidence that continued treatment would help. Of 20 cases reviewed, 15 were judged to involve unsatisfactory care and five required improvement.

segments.title: Patients seek answers
segments.body: One patient received more than 10 years of chemotherapy after being told they had a deadly tumour; the diagnosis was later found to be a low-grade tumour that did not require chemotherapy. The report recommends independent reviews for living patients treated with more than 12 cycles. Trust leaders apologised, while a law firm representing more than 40 patients has called for a public inquiry.

content.headline: Climate advisers warn weakening UK electric-car rules risks missing targets
content.shortHeadline: Weakening EV rules risks UK climate targets, advisers warn
content.standfirst: The Climate Change Committee says looser sales rules could add 8.4m tonnes of carbon dioxide a year by the next decade. The car industry disputes its assessment as ministers review the mandate.

sources.originalTitle: UK will miss climate targets if it weakens EV sales rules, advisers warn

segments.body: The Climate Change Committee says the UK is likely to miss its legally binding climate targets if ministers allow more sales of petrol and diesel cars and vans over the next four years. It estimates the changes could add 8.4m tonnes of carbon dioxide a year by the next decade.

segments.title: Industry challenges the assessment
segments.body: The committee says weakening the zero-emission vehicle mandate would require major emissions cuts elsewhere. The Society of Motor Manufacturers and Traders argues the rules impose costly discounts and deter investment. The government says it remains committed to ending sales of new petrol and diesel cars by 2030 and that its consultation will not change that commitment.

content.headline: UK-EU reset talks include youth mobility and medicine-supply cooperation
content.shortHeadline: UK-EU talks cover youth mobility and medicine supplies
content.standfirst: Draft plans point to a youth scheme and information-sharing on medicine shortages, alongside food-trade negotiations. The reported prospect of dropping a foie gras import ban has drawn criticism from animal-welfare groups.

sources.originalTitle: UK will ‘significantly reduce’ tuition fees for EU students if Brexit deal signed
Pharmacies to have better access to antibiotics and ADHD drugs in new Brexit deal
Ministers to drop foie gras imports ban to help seal EU food trade deal

segments.body: A draft UK-EU summit statement proposes working towards a youth-mobility scheme, potentially in place by 2028, though negotiations on its cap are ongoing. The draft also points to lower UK tuition fees for EU undergraduates, with talks to conclude within six months, and continued negotiations over UK access to the EU’s Made in Europe scheme.

segments.title: Medicine supplies and a welfare dispute
segments.body: A separate draft text describes cooperation on health security, including sharing information on drug shortages and how to source supplies. Meanwhile, ministers are expected to drop the promised foie gras import ban to help secure a food-trade agreement, according to the Guardian. Animal-welfare organisations criticised that reported change; the final terms of the package remain under negotiation.

perspectives.body: Animal-welfare charities say shelving the import ban would be a setback, arguing that closer trade ties should not come at the expense of protections against force-feeding ducks and geese.

content.headline: Israel postpones West Bank settlement tender amid UK sanctions
content.shortHeadline: Israel delays West Bank settlement tender amid sanctions
content.standfirst: Israel’s attorney general has ordered a delay to contracts for the E1 expansion, saying the caretaker government should not decide the issue. Israeli diplomats deny the move was a response to UK sanctions on settlement firms.

image.caption: Palestinian Bedouin boys play football near the area marked for the E1 settlement.

sources.originalTitle: Israel delays building contracts for West Bank settlement after UK sanctions

segments.body: Israel has postponed issuing contracts for more than 3,400 homes in the E1 settlement area of the occupied West Bank. Attorney general Gali Baharav-Miara instructed the land authority and housing ministry not to open the tender, saying the decision should be left to a future administration.

The delay came days after the UK sanctioned eight construction firms operating in the area. Israeli diplomats say the postponement was not a response to those sanctions. The E1 plan is controversial because its location between Jerusalem and Ma’aleh Adumim is seen as potentially dividing the West Bank and undermining a future Palestinian state.

content.headline: Research finds Reform councils’ promised cuts similar to other authorities
content.shortHeadline: Reform councils’ cuts broadly match other authorities, study finds
content.standfirst: An analysis of six Reform-majority county councils found that genuine discretionary savings were a similar share of budgets to those in comparable councils. The party disputes the comparison and says its changes are ongoing.

image.caption: Nigel Farage, who promised sweeping local-government cuts after Reform’s strong election performance.

sources.originalTitle: ‘In the end, nothing happened’: how Reform’s Doge-style crackdown fell flat

segments.body: Research by Public First Global found that six Reform-majority county councils had not cut spending faster or more deeply than comparable authorities. Of £254m in savings stated in their latest budgets, the analysis counted £30m–£44m as genuine discretionary cuts after excluding inherited savings, statutory-demand changes and income generation.

segments.title: Promises and constraints
segments.body: The study found no declared savings from promised cuts to net-zero or diversity initiatives. A former Reform councillor said the party’s local-government efficiency drive had fallen flat, while Reform’s local-government lead rejected the analysis as comparing unlike councils and said local authorities lack the powers for the approach the party wanted. The researchers say definitive spending figures are still some way off.

content.headline: Peter Kyle urges Labour to promise EU re-entry talks at next election
content.shortHeadline: Peter Kyle calls for Labour pledge to seek EU re-entry
content.standfirst: The former business secretary wants Labour to promise negotiations on rejoining the bloc, with a referendum on any final deal. His intervention comes as ministers prepare for a summit on closer UK-EU ties.

sources.originalTitle: Burnham should fight next election on promise to rejoin EU, says Peter Kyle

segments.body: Labour MP Peter Kyle says the party should campaign at the next general election on a commitment to begin negotiations to rejoin the EU, followed by a public vote on the agreed terms. He argues that a defined choice between the status quo and re-entry is preferable to an intermediate arrangement such as joining the customs union or single market.

Kyle’s call adds to pressure on Prime Minister Andy Burnham, who has said there is no rush to settle the UK’s long-term relationship with the bloc. The government is instead preparing near-term agreements on food and farming, emissions trading and youth mobility; Kyle says a referendum should follow any eventual re-entry deal.

content.headline: Man remanded over alleged DKK 34m tax fraud involving nicotine pouches
content.shortHeadline: Man remanded in alleged DKK 34m nicotine-pouch fraud
content.standfirst: A 27-year-old Danish citizen has been remanded for 27 days after police accused him and another man of evading at least DKK 34m in VAT and duties through importing and selling nicotine pouches.

sources.originalTitle: Varetægtsfængslet for millionsvindel med nikotinposer

segments.body: Copenhagen Police say a 27-year-old man was arrested at Copenhagen Airport on Tuesday and remanded for 27 days in a case involving the import and sale of nicotine pouches. He and a 28-year-old man, believed to be abroad, are suspected of depriving the state of at least DKK 34m in VAT and duties.
Police say they searched an address in Glostrup and seized 22 boxes of nicotine pouches. The second suspect has been remanded in absentia. The allegations have not been tested in court.

content.headline: Danish drivers to form emergency corridor when motorway traffic slows
content.shortHeadline: New Danish rule sets motorway emergency corridor
content.standfirst: Drivers must make a clear passage between lanes when traffic falls below 10km/h or stops. The national practice is intended to help emergency vehicles reach incidents more quickly.

image.caption: Vehicles form an emergency corridor on a Danish motorway in road-camera footage.

sources.originalTitle: Ny praksis på motorvejen skal få de blå blink hurtigere frem

segments.body: A new practice on Danish motorways tells drivers to form an emergency corridor as soon as traffic drops below 10km/h. Drivers in the far-left lane should move left; other drivers should move right, with those in the inside right lane allowed to use part of the hard shoulder.

The Road Directorate says emergency vehicles can struggle to pass when cars are positioned unpredictably in queues. Municipal emergency services have called for a common national approach. The practice applies even when no emergency vehicle is yet visible, since stopped traffic may indicate an incident ahead.

content.headline: Copenhagen politicians propose a 10km green park around the old city
content.shortHeadline: Copenhagen parties propose 10km green park
content.standfirst: Five parties at City Hall want to create a connected park following the route of the old 17th-century fortifications. Their first proposed step is a study of the project’s costs and timetable.

image.caption: Illustration of the proposed green route around Copenhagen’s historic centre.

sources.originalTitle: Politikere vil lave 10 kilometer lang grøn park rundt om det ældste København

segments.body: A political majority at Copenhagen City Hall wants to explore a 10km green park around the historic centre, following the route of the city’s 17th-century fortifications. The proposed route would connect existing green spaces including the ramparts at Christianshavn, Østre Anlæg and Kastellet.

segments.title: Traffic and the next step
segments.body: Supporters say Copenhagen needs more green space and that parts of the route, including H.C. Andersens Boulevard, may need to change. Conservative politician Jakob Næsager supports the idea of a green ring but says cars must still be able to pass through it. The parties’ first step is to commission a study of the cost and timeline.

content.headline: Lidl recalls frozen-capable duck products over salmonella risk
content.shortHeadline: Lidl recalls duck products over salmonella risk
content.standfirst: The recall covers Butcher’s duck breast fillets and legs with a 11 November 2026 use-by date. The date has passed, but customers who froze the products are advised to discard or return them.

sources.originalTitle: Lidl tilbagekalder pekingand på grund af risiko for salmonella

segments.body: Lidl is recalling a batch of Butcher’s Peking duck products because of a possible salmonella risk. The affected items are breast fillets and legs with a use-by date of 11 November 2026.
Although the use-by date has passed, the retailer says some customers may have frozen the products. Anyone who still has them should discard them or return them to a Lidl store.

content.headline: Stolen Fiat 500 found after owner’s social-media appeal
content.shortHeadline: Viral appeal helps owner recover stolen Fiat
content.standfirst: Rikki Vanggaard’s 18-year-old car was found in Bording 13 days after it disappeared in Herning. Police suggested she use Facebook to seek information; a local woman recognised the car.

sources.originalTitle: Efterlysning gav pote: Rikki forenet med sin elskede Fiat

segments.body: Rikki Vanggaard’s Fiat 500 was stolen from Herning shortly after repairs. She posted an appeal on Facebook after police suggested asking her network for help, and a young woman in Bording recognised the car at the railway station 25 kilometres away.

The car was returned after 13 days, though its red leather seats had been damaged. Police stressed that investigating crime is not the public’s responsibility; the Facebook suggestion was offered as an additional way to look for the unusually distinctive car.

content.headline: Glastonbury names Sam Fender, Harry Styles and Billie Eilish as 2027 headliners
content.shortHeadline: Glastonbury 2027: Fender, Styles and Eilish lead the bill
content.standfirst: The festival’s first lineup announcement also includes Cher in the legends slot and debuts for Kraftwerk and Angine de Poitrine. One critic argues that its trio of Pyramid Stage headliners lacks variety.

image.caption: Billie Eilish, Harry Styles and Sam Fender, Glastonbury’s 2027 headliners.

sources.originalTitle: Sam Fender, Harry Styles and Billie Eilish to be youngest Glastonbury headliners of 21st century
Why Glastonbury can’t get good headliners

segments.body: Sam Fender, Harry Styles and Billie Eilish will headline Glastonbury’s Pyramid Stage next June. It is a first top-billing at the festival for Fender and Styles; Eilish returns after headlining in 2022. Cher is booked for the Sunday legends slot, while Kraftwerk and Angine de Poitrine are among the acts making their festival debuts.

segments.title: A question of balance
segments.body: The first announcement also includes the xx, Lily Allen, Little Simz, Massive Attack and FKA twigs, alongside artists spanning pop, rock, rap and dance. Tickets have sold out; the article says the 2027 price of £408, including a booking fee, is the festival’s first above £400.

The i Paper’s critic says the headliners are individually worthy but too similar in audience and career stage to make a compelling trio. The view is that Glastonbury’s scale and reputation should make room for more contrast and risk.

perspectives.body: The i Paper offers a pointed counter-reading of the lineup: the headliners may be popular, but the critic sees their shared audience and relative career stage as a missed chance to make the Pyramid bill feel more distinctive.

content.headline: Grammys 2027: Raye leads nominations as Beyoncé reaches 100
content.shortHeadline: Raye leads Grammys nominations; Beyoncé reaches 100
content.standfirst: Raye has 11 nominations, with Rosalía on nine and Olivia Rodrigo among the other leading contenders. The newly introduced Asian pop category has already drawn criticism from BTS.

image.caption: Raye performing at the Greek Theatre in Los Angeles in May 2026.

sources.originalTitle: Grammys 2027: Raye, Rosalía and Olivia Rodrigo lead female-heavy nominations

segments.body: Raye leads the 2027 Grammy nominations with 11, including nods for album, song and songwriter of the year. Rosalía has nine nominations, while Olivia Rodrigo, Phoebe Bridgers, Miranda Lambert and Ella Langley each have seven. Beyoncé has received her 100th nomination and remains the ceremony’s most nominated and most awarded artist.

segments.title: New categories, new arguments
segments.body: BTS declined to submit music for the new best Asian pop performance category, saying they hope their work can be heard without being divided by region or language. The ceremony is scheduled for 7 February in Los Angeles; a host has not yet been announced.

content.headline: Bobby Charles’s songs found a way from the bayou to the Band
content.shortHeadline: Bobby Charles, the bayou songwriter who rarely took the stage
content.standfirst: A career-spanning box set revisits the Cajun songwriter whose work was recorded by Fats Domino and Etta James and whose own music remained overlooked. Friends remember an original voice and a fierce defender of the Louisiana wetlands.

image.caption: Bobby Charles, date unknown.

sources.originalTitle: ‘Everything he said sounded like a song title!’ The rackety, romantic life of Bobby Charles, alligator-befriending bard of the bayou

segments.body: Bobby Charles wrote songs recorded by Fats Domino, Etta James and others, despite being unable to play an instrument. Signed to Chess Records as a teenager, he came close to early rock’n’roll stardom, but chose a reclusive life and rarely performed. A new career-spanning box set aims to bring his recordings back into view.

segments.title: A songwriter on his own terms
segments.body: Charles’s “See You Later, Alligator” became a hit, but its success was followed by racism and threats during a tour with Chuck Berry. He turned increasingly to songwriting for other artists. Later, his work with members of the Band and Dr John produced records that friends and collaborators describe as soulful, inventive and too little heard.

In his later years, Charles wrote about pollution and the loss of Louisiana’s coastline. He was furious at oil companies and those dumping waste in the Mississippi River, according to LCD Soundsystem’s Korey Richey, who knew him. Charles died in 2010; a session with Dr John titled “Solution for Pollution” remains unreleased.

content.headline: Echo & the Bunnymen return with an album shaped by Ian McCulloch
content.shortHeadline: Ian McCulloch on Echo & the Bunnymen’s new album
content.standfirst: Apples for Isaac is the band’s first album in 12 years, largely written and played by McCulloch. The singer discusses its renewed energy and his strained creative relationship with guitarist Will Sergeant.

image.caption: Ian McCulloch of Echo & the Bunnymen.

sources.originalTitle: Ian McCulloch: ‘Will Sergeant isn’t the heart of Echo & The Bunnymen. He’s the spleen’

segments.body: Echo & the Bunnymen have released Apples for Isaac, their first album in 12 years. Ian McCulloch says he wrote and produced it himself and played most of the instruments, with drummer Clem Burke on most tracks. He calls the record lively and says he is pleased with how it turned out.

segments.title: A band under strain
segments.body: Guitarist Will Sergeant plays on four tracks. McCulloch dismisses the suggestion that the album is a solo record, but says the pair have not always agreed on the music and describes some submitted parts as unsuitable. Sergeant has previously spoken of a long-standing undercurrent of animosity and feeling excluded from songwriting.

content.headline: Chxrry’s debut turns self-belief into high-octane R&B pop
content.shortHeadline: Chxrry’s brash, playful debut gets a deluxe edition
content.standfirst: U, Me & My Ego moves between glossy synth-pop, R&B and breakup ballads, with a forceful personality at its centre. Pitchfork finds the bonus tracks less essential than the original album.

sources.originalTitle: U, Me & My Ego (Deluxe)

segments.body: Toronto singer Chxrry builds her debut around swagger, theatrical hooks and 2010s R&B-pop gloss. Its starting point was “Main Character”, whose hook gathered attention on TikTok. Across the album she mixes brash songs such as “Groupie” with more vulnerable moments, including the ballad “Boring” and “Bottles & Lights”, a duet with Mariah the Scientist.

Pitchfork describes the deluxe edition as more of an outfit change than an upgrade, finding its new songs uneven. The review singles out “Friends Don’t Kiss” as the strongest bonus track, but argues that the album’s appeal rests on Chxrry’s forceful, unvarnished character.

content.headline: Snoh Aalegra brings Minneapolis funk to an album of uncertain love
content.shortHeadline: Snoh Aalegra’s sleek, yearning Legendary Love
content.standfirst: The Swedish Iranian singer draws directly on the Minneapolis sound, working with Jimmy Jam and Terry Lewis among others. Pitchfork praises the ambition while finding some of its polished production too smooth.

sources.originalTitle: Legendary Love

segments.body: On Legendary Love, Snoh Aalegra draws on the funk and new-wave blend known as the Minneapolis sound, associated with her mentor Prince. The album uses analogue synthesisers and drum machines, and brings in producers Jimmy Jam and Terry Lewis. Its songs trace a romantic connection that remains intense but never settles into certainty.

segments.title: Gloss and heartache
segments.body: Pitchfork highlights “I Love You” for its shifting vocal delivery and contributions from Nile Rodgers and Raphael Saadiq. But the review also finds that the record’s immaculate arrangements can smooth away some of the friction in its heartbreak. It calls the album Aalegra’s most ambitious and affecting yet, while sensing room for more surprise.

content.headline: Cute turn noise-rock into five long, slow-building songs of dread
content.shortHeadline: Cute’s debut album makes noise tell a story
content.standfirst: The Canadian quartet’s first album shapes its sludgegaze into patient, escalating compositions. Pitchfork hears a record that confronts political unease and private turmoil, while leaving room for endurance.

sources.originalTitle: history is not woven by innocent hands

segments.body: Cute’s debut, history is not woven by innocent hands, distils the Hamilton quartet’s sprawling noise-rock into five tracks of roughly 10 minutes each. Their music builds slowly, using distortion and repetition not just for impact but to shape each song’s movement from tension toward eruption.

segments.title: A way through the darkness
segments.body: Pitchfork reads the title as a response to geopolitical unrest and oligarchic power, but says songwriter Daniel Conroy is more concerned with the damage that crisis and insecurity do inside people. The review finds the most forceful statement in “force majeure”, where a rare first-person confession turns the album’s caustic sound toward melancholy and the possibility of carrying on.

content.headline: Heavensouls turns digital overload into a restless, searching collage
content.shortHeadline: Heavensouls makes a collage of collages on cantu of the sower
content.standfirst: The 20-year-old producer combines free-jazz thinking, electronic fragments and live instruments on an album-length EP shaped by his movement between Nigeria and the online world.

sources.originalTitle: cantu of the sower EP

segments.body: On cantu of the sower, producer heavensouls—Chidi Obialo—layers flickering electronic sounds with saxophone, strings, guitar and percussion. The nearly nine-minute “today is my favorite” captures the EP’s method: a crowded, shifting soundscape that gradually makes room for a gentle, wistful calm.

segments.title: A crowded inner landscape
segments.body: Pitchfork connects the project’s restless collage to Obialo’s life moving between Nigeria, the suburbs and internet music communities. A sample on “model housing” calls for liberation and challenges capitalism; elsewhere, the music moves between anxiety, humour and longing. The review hears a search for emotional space rather than a collage of sounds for its own sake.

content.headline: Robert Pattinson’s Bond casting brings star power—and questions of control
content.shortHeadline: Pattinson’s Bond: a big-name choice with baggage
content.standfirst: Reports say Josh O’Connor withdrew from the contest, while Jeff Bezos says he helped choose Pattinson. Critics question whether an established franchise star can make Bond feel fresh.

image.caption: Robert Pattinson, who has been cast as James Bond.

sources.originalTitle: Shaken and stirred: Jeff Bezos says he was ‘heavily involved’ in picking new James Bond
Bond role was ‘Josh O’Connor’s to lose’ but actor pulled out of the running, report suggests
The big problem with Robert Pattinson playing Bond
The first truly weird Bond: 13 things to know about Robert Pattinson – from heavy saliva to dead clowns

segments.body: Jeff Bezos says he was heavily involved in casting Robert Pattinson as James Bond, and that the actor stood out in screen tests despite an initial preference for an unknown. Amazon gained creative control of the franchise last year, a shift that has prompted questions about how the company may shape its future.

segments.title: The choice—and the alternatives
segments.body: A report in Puck’s What I’m Hearing newsletter says Josh O’Connor was an early favourite of director Denis Villeneuve but pulled out after having reservations about the role. The i Paper’s critic argues that Pattinson’s fame and existing franchise roles could make it harder for him to disappear into Bond, while acknowledging the actor’s range between blockbusters and art-house films.

perspectives.body: The i Paper questions whether an actor already identified with major franchises can offer Bond a genuinely fresh start, and whether the role will make sufficient use of Pattinson’s range.

segments.body: A Guardian profile presents Pattinson as an unpredictable performer whose odd public persona has helped make him an unusual choice for the most mainstream of roles. The script, supporting cast and production timetable remain unresolved in the gathered reporting.

content.headline: Josephine review: a child witnesses violence in a drama that takes big risks
content.shortHeadline: Josephine review: a child’s trauma, and a striking performance
content.standfirst: Mason Reeves is compelling as an eight-year-old who witnesses a rape, but the review finds parts of Beth de Araújo’s drama contrived and its treatment of the trial unresolved.

image.caption: Channing Tatum as Damien and Mason Reeves as Josephine.

sources.originalTitle: Josephine review – Channing Tatum and Gemma Chan ballast knotty drama about a child witness to a rape

segments.body: Beth de Araújo’s film follows Josephine, played by newcomer Mason Reeves, after she witnesses a rape in a San Francisco park. The experience unsettles her, while her parents struggle to understand how to help and the prospect of her giving evidence in court draws closer. The review praises Reeves’s performance but warns that the film’s subject matter makes for difficult viewing.

segments.title: A forceful film, with doubts
segments.body: The review finds powerful moments in Josephine’s disorientation, but says the repeated appearance of the rapist as a silent figure can feel contrived. It also questions the film’s decision to leave the verdict unseen, arguing that the outcome would matter in the real world even if the family must continue living with the trauma.

content.headline: Nathan Fielder’s comedy turns awkwardness into a study of truth
content.shortHeadline: Nathan Fielder’s strange, meticulous comedy
content.standfirst: With You Can See Everything reaching UK cinemas, a look back at how Fielder moved from elaborate business pranks to a comedy that blurs performance, documentary and human connection.

image.caption: Nathan Fielder in The Rehearsal.

sources.originalTitle: From Dumb Starbucks to dada documentary: everything you need to know about Nathan Fielder

segments.body: Nathan Fielder first drew a wider audience with Nathan for You, playing an exaggerated version of himself as he devised outlandish schemes for struggling businesses. The series grew beyond its mock-business premise into elaborate performance, including an attempt to recreate a bar’s ordinary night as a play.

segments.title: From rehearsal to reality
segments.body: The Guardian traces the method from those early set-ups through The Rehearsal, where Fielder and his collaborators stage scenarios to anticipate how people might react. The new three-hour film You Can See Everything follows Elizabeth Holmes in the lead-up to prison, and is described as a meditation on truth and how little we can know about other people.

content.headline: Your Mother Your Mother Your Mother review: a hitman’s unlikely family crisis
content.shortHeadline: Your Mother Your Mother Your Mother review: a killer in crisis
content.standfirst: Mahershala Ali plays a devout Muslim hitman who must care for his children after his wife dies. The review enjoys the film’s comic energy but questions the tension between faith and violence.

image.caption: Mahershala Ali and John Cho in Your Mother Your Mother Your Mother.

sources.originalTitle: Your Mother Your Mother Your Mother review – Mahershala Ali’s religious hitman on the hunt for baby milk

segments.body: In Bassam Tariq’s thriller, Mahershala Ali plays Latif, a contract killer whose wife’s death leaves him responsible for their children, including a newborn who cannot drink formula. As he tries to find breast milk, his employer presses him to accept another killing. The Guardian describes the film as boisterous, colourful and blackly comic.

segments.title: The limits of the joke
segments.body: The review sees shades of John Woo and Quentin Tarantino in the action, and praises the performances. But it questions the film’s handling of Latif’s religious convictions: a devout Muslim who makes his living as a paid killer, in a story where mothers and other women have little influence.

content.headline: The Social Reckoning review: a chilling sequel about Facebook’s power
content.shortHeadline: The Social Reckoning turns Facebook’s past into present dread
content.standfirst: Aaron Sorkin’s follow-up revisits the Facebook Files and the company’s handling of its own research. The review finds a tense investigative drama—and an uncomfortable mirror of everyday reliance on Meta.

image.caption: Jeremy Strong as Mark Zuckerberg in The Social Reckoning.

sources.originalTitle: I was terrified watching The Social Reckoning – then went back to scrolling

segments.body: The Social Reckoning turns to the Facebook Files, the reporting that exposed internal research into the platform’s effects and its role in spreading misinformation. Jeremy Allen White plays journalist Jeff Horwitz and Mikey Madison plays whistleblower Frances Haugen; Jeremy Strong is Mark Zuckerberg.

segments.title: The unease after the credits
segments.body: The i Paper’s critic describes the film as an investigative thriller that also feels like horror, arguing that the company’s incentives can amplify anger and keep people scrolling. The review’s personal complication is that the writer, like many users, still relies on Meta products despite the misgivings the film raises.

content.headline: Elsinore revisits Ian Charleson’s Hamlet as he was dying of Aids
content.shortHeadline: Elsinore recalls Ian Charleson’s final, extraordinary Hamlet
content.standfirst: Andrew Scott plays the actor who took on Hamlet at the National Theatre while living with Aids. People who knew Charleson describe the performance’s physical cost and the support around his final run.

sources.originalTitle: 'A hell of a thing to take on': The moving inside story of how Ian Charleson played Hamlet on stage while dying of Aids
Elsinore to The Hunger Games: 12 of the best films to watch in November

segments.body: In 1989, Ian Charleson took over as Hamlet at London’s National Theatre while living with Aids. Elsinore, a film about that final stage role, stars Andrew Scott. The BBC’s account draws on interviews with Charleson’s friend Sean Mathias, his doctor Margaret Johnson and fellow actor Paul Jesson.

segments.title: The work behind the performance
segments.body: Charleson gave 24 performances before his final appearance in November 1989 and died a few weeks later, aged 40. Jesson says Scott’s portrayal is deeply affecting, while recalling that Charleson was physically weaker than the film’s version. Johnson, meanwhile, says she never urged him to give up the role.

Charleson’s final performance helped make his illness more publicly visible. His wishes were followed in announcing that he had died of Aids. The specialist clinic at the Royal Free Hospital was later renamed the Ian Charleson Day Centre.

content.headline: 14 film flops that deserve a second look
content.shortHeadline: Fourteen box-office failures worth revisiting
content.standfirst: From The Thing and Dune to Babylon and Furiosa, this guide argues that commercial failure need not be the last word on a film’s reputation.

image.caption: A selection of films the article argues are worth revisiting.

sources.originalTitle: The 14 spectacular film flops that are actually worth watching

segments.body: The i Paper revisits 14 films that underperformed or were rejected on release but have since drawn reassessment. The list ranges from Michael Cimino’s Heaven’s Gate and David Lynch’s Dune to The Thing, Last Action Hero, Dredd, Cloud Atlas and Babylon.

segments.title: Failure is not the whole story
segments.body: The cases vary: some were ambitious projects that struggled to find an audience, while others gained supporters over time. The article suggests timing, expectations and a film’s eventual cultural life can matter as much as its first box-office result.

content.headline: Heated Rivalry fans take the show’s sex scenes to 4DX
content.shortHeadline: Heated Rivalry in 4DX: fans embrace the daft, damp spectacle
content.standfirst: Cineworld screenings add moving seats, wind and water to episodes of the queer hockey drama. Fans say the effects make for a hilarious night out, though some moments interrupt the emotional pull.

image.caption: Connor Storrie as Ilya Rozanov and Hudson Williams as Shane Hollander in Heated Rivalry.

sources.originalTitle: ‘I hope paramedics are on standby for the sex scenes!’ The wet and wild TV experience leaving fans dizzy

segments.body: Fans of Heated Rivalry have been watching episodes five and six in 4DX, a format usually used for action films. The screenings add motion, gusts of air and sprays of water to the hockey drama’s romance, turning texts, icy encounters and bedroom scenes into part of the cinema’s sensory effects.

segments.title: A knowingly silly night out
segments.body: The Guardian’s reporter and the fans interviewed describe the screening as chaotic and funny. One viewer says the effects sometimes distracted from the emotional story, but several fans enjoyed the novelty and said they would go again.

content.headline: Joanna Page describes an unnamed actor’s inappropriate behaviour
content.shortHeadline: Joanna Page speaks about inappropriate behaviour on set
content.standfirst: The Gavin and Stacey actor said an unnamed male colleague whispered offensive comments before takes. Page has previously described being groped by a television host but did not identify him.

image.caption: Joanna Page, who is appearing on I’m a Celebrity … Get Me Out of Here!

sources.originalTitle: Joanna Page says ‘inappropriate’ male actor whispered ‘awful stuff’ to her

segments.body: Joanna Page said on I’m a Celebrity that an unnamed actor whispered “inappropriate” and “awful” things to her before a take, including chanting about what he would do to her during a scene. She said nobody intervened and that speaking up felt difficult.

Page has previously said she was groped by an unnamed male television host after a producer warned her he was “very handsy”. Her comments come amid renewed scrutiny of abuse and power in the TV industry. The gathered report does not name the actor or identify the production she was discussing.

content.headline: The Last Spy review: a century of history through a CIA officer’s eyes
content.shortHeadline: The Last Spy follows a remarkable life—and leaves questions open
content.standfirst: Peter Sichel tells the story of his escape from Nazi Germany and work for US intelligence. The review finds the documentary compelling, though it says his later career becomes less personal and leaves key secrets unresolved.

image.caption: Peter Sichel, whose account anchors The Last Spy.

sources.originalTitle: The Last Spy review – a riveting tale of CIA meddling, espionage gossip and Blue Nun wine

segments.body: Katharina Otto-Bernstein’s documentary centres on Peter Sichel, a German Jewish refugee who joined the US army and later worked for the Office of Strategic Services and the CIA. Filmed when he was 100, his account follows his escape from Europe, intelligence work in Berlin and a career that placed him close to Cold War decision-making.

segments.title: The secrets left untold
segments.body: The Guardian calls Sichel’s personal account riveting but says the film becomes more impersonal as it moves into geopolitical history. Sichel reveals that he left the CIA because he believed agents were repeatedly being sent to their deaths, but does not tell his family or viewers what he and his agents did in the field.

content.headline: Young, British and Tradwife review: a movement that needs more scrutiny
content.shortHeadline: Young, British and Tradwife leaves big questions hanging
content.standfirst: Poppy Jay meets three women with different relationships to the tradwife ideal. The review praises her questioning of the men but wishes the film probed the women’s motives and circumstances further.

image.caption: Molly with her husband Aaron and their children in Young, British and Tradwife.

sources.originalTitle: Young, British and Tradwife review – TV this frustrating should come with a blood pressure warning

segments.body: In Young, British and Tradwife, film-maker Poppy Jay meets three women who advocate or live by the lifestyle in Britain. They include Megan, who makes money through social-media content involving her children, and Laura Zachary, who says she treats her husband “like he’s Jesus”.

segments.title: What the film cannot settle
segments.body: The Guardian’s reviewer says Jay is formidable when questioning the men but too careful with some of the women. The review wants more scrutiny of how online income, business choices and personal history shape the women’s accounts, and describes the hour as a starting point for deeper investigation rather than a conclusive portrait.

content.headline: The Altruists review: a tech-fraud romance arrives with timely questions
content.shortHeadline: The Altruists revisits the FTX scandal and its idealists
content.standfirst: Netflix’s drama follows Sam Bankman-Fried and Caroline Ellison as FTX rises and collapses. The Guardian finds the series a little dated, but its portrait of risk-loving tech idealists still feels relevant.

image.caption: Julia Garner as Caroline Ellison and Anthony Boyle as Sam Bankman-Fried in The Altruists.

sources.originalTitle: The Altruists to Yellowjackets: the seven best shows to stream this week

segments.body: The Altruists dramatises the relationship between FTX founder Sam Bankman-Fried, played by Anthony Boyle, and Caroline Ellison, played by Julia Garner. The series follows the pair’s rise and the collapse of the cryptocurrency exchange, drawing on a scandal that has already inspired several screen accounts of technology leaders.
The Guardian’s streaming guide finds the drama somewhat staid, but says its story of tech idealism mixed with extreme risk-taking feels pertinent. The show begins streaming on Netflix on 19 November.

content.headline: Danny Robins on ghosts, fear and his new drama The Witch Farm
content.shortHeadline: Danny Robins keeps an open mind about ghosts
content.standfirst: The Uncanny host says he still has not seen a ghost, despite being drawn to stories that leave believers and sceptics asking different questions. His podcast The Witch Farm is now a BBC drama.

image.caption: Danny Robins, host of Uncanny and writer of The Witch Farm.

sources.originalTitle: Danny Robins: ‘My wife has never listened to Uncanny. She finds it terrifying’

segments.body: Danny Robins’s podcast The Witch Farm, based on accounts of a haunting in rural Wales, has been adapted as a four-part BBC drama. He says he does not claim ghosts are real, but remains interested in the experiences people describe and in the uncertainty those stories leave behind.

segments.title: Believers and sceptics in the same room
segments.body: Robins says Uncanny works for listeners who treat the stories as mysteries to solve and for those who ask how the experiences might have happened. He is careful about accounts involving vulnerability and mental health, and contrasts his approach with paranormal shows that present supernatural explanations as fact.

content.headline: Russell Brand: Open Secret review revisits the culture that enabled him
content.shortHeadline: Open Secret asks how Russell Brand’s behaviour went unchecked
content.standfirst: The documentary brings together reporting, interviews and archive footage after Brand’s rape conviction. The review argues that its most disturbing point is how widely his behaviour was tolerated.

image.caption: Russell Brand in Netflix’s Open Secret.

sources.originalTitle: Netflix’s Russell Brand documentary feels like a horror film

segments.body: Netflix’s Open Secret traces Russell Brand’s rise and the reporting that led to his conviction for rape and sexual assault. It includes interviews with journalists who investigated the allegations, people who knew Brand and women who describe their experiences.

segments.title: A culture in view
segments.body: The i Paper’s reviewer says the film’s most unsettling argument is not simply that Brand behaved abusively, but that his public persona and conduct were often treated as acceptable by audiences and parts of the industry. The documentary also includes testimony from women; the article distinguishes their accounts from the conviction and reporting it describes.

content.headline: Black Doves returns, still mixing spy games with moral unease
content.shortHeadline: Black Doves returns with more violence and uneasy loyalties
content.standfirst: Keira Knightley and Joe Barton discuss season two of the Netflix thriller, in which a spy’s family life and body count collide. The creators describe the show’s balance of comedy and the consequences of violence.

image.caption: Keira Knightley as Helen Webb in Black Doves.

sources.originalTitle: Keira Knightley on Black Doves: ‘The violence is like a video game’

segments.body: Black Doves returns with Helen Webb, played by Keira Knightley, facing riskier missions while her husband’s political career advances. Helen’s handler has disappeared, and Sam, played by Ben Whishaw, is working through a kill list in exchange for freedom.

segments.title: The people behind the body count
segments.body: Knightley calls the violence almost like a video game, but says the story brings individual deaths into focus. Creator Joe Barton argues that audiences readily accept violence from familiar genre heroes such as James Bond, and says the series tries to acknowledge the moral grey area while keeping its characters compelling.

content.headline: GTA VI review: a vast crime world with room for an unlikely love story
content.shortHeadline: GTA VI: a sprawling world that makes you care
content.standfirst: Rockstar’s new game pairs its familiar excess with a more intimate story about fugitive couple Jason and Lucia. The review finds a world of astonishing detail, though its controls and collisions can frustrate.

image.caption: Jason and Lucia, the central couple in Grand Theft Auto VI.

sources.originalTitle: Grand Theft Auto VI review – gaming’s most depraved world is now also its greatest love story

segments.body: GTA VI sends players into Leonida, a detailed fictional Florida, through Jason and Lucia, a criminal couple trying to build a life while getting pulled into trouble. The Guardian’s review describes a world full of side activities and small observations, from gyms and shops to wildlife and passing conversations.

segments.title: More than chaos
segments.body: The review says the game gives players reasons to care about Jason and Lucia, with small rewards for acts of kindness alongside its trademark violence and crude humour. Lucia is the series’ first female protagonist; the reviewer says women in the game feel more like people, while cautioning that GTA VI is not thereby a feminist game.

The world’s realism can make play unwieldy. Controls are complex, missions can go wrong in confusing ways, and the game sometimes seems to work against the player. Even so, the reviewer says the bond between its leads gives the sprawling game a strong emotional centre.

content.headline: GTA Online players mark the end of an era with one last drive
content.shortHeadline: GTA Online players gather for one last drive
content.standfirst: As GTA VI arrives, players are organising peaceful convoys through Los Santos. For some, the decade-old game is not only a criminal sandbox but also a place where friendships have grown.

image.caption: Grand Theft Auto V, the game world players are gathering to revisit.

sources.originalTitle: Players say goodbye to Grand Theft Auto V with one last drive

segments.body: Players organised final-drive events across GTA Online before GTA VI’s release, taking convoys through the game’s Los Santos and surrounding countryside. The normally combative multiplayer world was, for the occasion, a place to drive together rather than fight.

segments.title: More than a game world
segments.body: One organiser, Willy, says he has played for 13 years and made close friends through online events. Another participant is taking part in memory of a friend he met in the game, while saying he plans to remain in Los Santos for a while after GTA VI launches.

content.headline: The Wii and PS3 imagined two futures for gaming—and both arrived
content.shortHeadline: Wii and PS3: two visions of gaming that still shape play
content.standfirst: Twenty years after their launch, Nintendo’s accessible motion controls and Sony’s technical ambition both look influential. The Guardian’s retrospective finds the consoles’ contrasting ideas survived, even as each had limits.

image.caption: Nintendo’s Wii and Sony’s PlayStation 3.

sources.originalTitle: Twenty years ago, the Wii and PS3 predicted the future of gaming – did they get it right?

segments.body: The Wii and PlayStation 3 launched in November 2006 with contrasting ideas about games. Nintendo favoured accessible hardware and motion controls, while Sony pursued technical power, online play and long, demanding adventures.

segments.title: Two legacies
segments.body: The Guardian’s retrospective argues that both approaches helped shape the industry: accessible play has continued through mobile games and Nintendo’s later consoles, while the PS3’s technical ambition and large-scale adventures helped set a different path. Neither vision proved complete, and both consoles also supported experiences that did not fit their headline identities.

content.headline: GTA’s radio stations turned game soundtracks into cultural destinations
content.shortHeadline: How GTA’s radio stations made game soundtracks matter
content.standfirst: Artists and curators recall how Rockstar’s real-world music choices shaped players’ memories and careers. The series’ growing reach has also brought questions about licensing and ownership.

image.caption: Jason and Lucia in Grand Theft Auto VI, the latest game in the series.

sources.originalTitle: Killer tunes: how Grand Theft Auto conquered the music world

segments.body: The Grand Theft Auto series began with fictional radio music, then brought real artists into its stations. Contributors describe how the changing sounds of places such as San Andreas and Vice City became part of players’ memories—and how hearing their own work in a GTA game could feel surreal.

segments.title: Reach and rights
segments.body: Flying Lotus says San Andreas made him feel that the game recognised Black culture; he later curated a station for GTA V. Nite Jewel says a track made for the game helped her return to independent music, but Rockstar owns its copyright under the reported work-for-hire arrangement. She says the continuing income is welcome, while acknowledging the terms are not an uncomplicated question of fairness.

content.headline: A veteran gamer finds himself inside an independent horror game
content.shortHeadline: From GamesMaster to game character, after 50 years of play
content.standfirst: Dominik Diamond is voicing a survival-horror hero in an independently made project. He writes about the oddness of hearing himself in the game—and the joy of showing it to his children.

image.caption: Draga, the character voiced by Dominik Diamond in Black Tides Draga’s Wake.

sources.originalTitle: After 50 years of playing video games, I’m finally starring in one

segments.body: After five decades playing games, writer and former GamesMaster presenter Dominik Diamond is voicing the lead in Black Tides Draga’s Wake. The survival-horror game, set on a decaying steamship, is being made by a small team working from different parts of the world.

segments.title: A personal performance
segments.body: Diamond describes adjusting his voice to fit the character and improvising combat sounds in the studio. Playing the game feels strange because the hero looks and sounds like him, but his favourite moment came when his children recognised their father in the character.

content.headline: BioWare’s closure leaves Mass Effect fans mourning a vanished future
content.shortHeadline: BioWare’s closure is a loss for role-playing games
content.standfirst: The cancellation of a new Mass Effect and the loss of more than 400 jobs have left one longtime fan reflecting on the trilogy’s lasting impact and the studio’s recent difficulties.

image.caption: Mass Effect 3, part of BioWare’s original trilogy.

sources.originalTitle: EA has closed BioWare – and Mass Effect fans like me are bereft

segments.body: The Guardian’s writer says EA has closed BioWare, cancelled its forthcoming Mass Effect game and left more than 400 people losing their jobs. The studio was known for role-playing games including Mass Effect, Dragon Age and Star Wars: Knights of the Old Republic.

segments.title: A world shaped by choices
segments.body: Writing as a longtime fan, the author recalls how the original Mass Effect trilogy combined a galaxy-spanning story with choices that changed relationships and later events. The essay mourns the possibility of another game while acknowledging that BioWare had not delivered a critical or commercial hit in more than a decade.

content.headline: Voyager 1 reaches one light-day from Earth after 49 years in space
content.shortHeadline: Voyager 1 is now one light-day from Earth
content.standfirst: The farthest human-made object is now 16.1bn miles away, making its radio signals a full day’s journey each way. Its milestone also renews the perspective offered by the mission’s famous view of Earth.

image.caption: Earth appears as a fraction of a pixel in Voyager 1’s “Pale Blue Dot” image.

sources.originalTitle: NASA’s Voyager 1 probe is now 1 light-day away
After 49 years, Nasa’s Voyager 1 is one light-day away from us. Can we save this ‘pale blue dot’?

segments.body: Voyager 1 crossed the one-light-day mark on 18 November, travelling about 16.1bn miles from Earth. It is the first human-made object to reach that distance; radio signals now take 24 hours to get there and another 24 hours to return. The spacecraft is still operating and sending readings on plasma waves, magnetic fields and space particles.

segments.title: A distant view of home
segments.body: The milestone recalls the probe’s 1990 image of Earth, the “pale blue dot”, in which the planet appears as a fraction of a pixel. Kim Heacox’s essay uses that image to turn the mission’s long journey into a reflection on humanity’s responsibility to protect its only known home.

perspectives.body: Heacox argues that the image should prompt people to preserve Earth and treat one another more kindly, setting the achievement of space exploration against the damage humans have done to ecosystems and the climate.

content.headline: Alzheimer’s pill slows decline by 31% in a trial subgroup, study suggests
content.shortHeadline: Alzheimer’s pill shows promise, but results need scrutiny
content.standfirst: A phase-three trial found slower decline among early Alzheimer’s patients taking AR1001 without other Alzheimer’s drugs. The result was not statistically significant across the wider group, and further trials and regulatory review are needed.

image.caption: Brain scans comparing metabolic patterns in Alzheimer’s patient cases.

sources.originalTitle: Pill that mimics Viagra can slow Alzheimer’s progression, study suggests

segments.body: The drug AR1001 slowed cognitive decline by 31% in 604 people with early Alzheimer’s who were not taking other Alzheimer’s medicines, according to results from a phase-three trial spanning 13 countries. The findings were presented at a conference; the drug’s South Korean maker, AriBio, reported the result.

segments.title: A promising result, not a treatment yet
segments.body: AR1001 belongs to the same family of medicines as Viagra and is being developed to relax blood vessels and increase blood flow to the brain. In a wider group of trial participants taking other Alzheimer’s drugs, the result was not statistically significant. Experts called the findings encouraging but said the data need scientific and regulatory scrutiny before the drug could be prescribed for Alzheimer’s.

content.headline: £9.3m study will examine effects of England’s planned under-16s social-media ban
content.shortHeadline: Study will test what an under-16s social-media ban changes
content.standfirst: Ten projects will follow more than 300,000 young people as researchers examine mental health, sleep, activity and family life before and after the planned UK restrictions. The work is intended to test effects, not assume them.

image.caption: The UK plans to restrict social-media access for under-16s from spring 2027.

sources.originalTitle: £10m ‘once-in-a-generation’ study to explore effects of children’s social media ban

segments.body: Researchers funded by Wellcome plan to study how the UK’s expected spring 2027 social-media restrictions for under-16s affect young people. The £9.3m programme brings together ten projects and more than 300,000 young people across Britain, in what researchers describe as the first study of its kind.

segments.title: What the research will track
segments.body: Projects will examine outcomes including mental health, sleep, physical activity, education and family relationships. One study will look at whether risky material moves between platforms; others will investigate workarounds and whether effects differ by gender, social class or sexual orientation. Researchers say the question is not simply whether social media is good or bad, but what changes when young people’s digital environment changes.

content.headline: Inquiry finds Derry bog body was a young woman beheaded over 2,000 years ago
content.shortHeadline: Derry bog body was a young woman beheaded in the Iron Age
content.standfirst: A coroner-led investigation found the Ballymacombs More Woman was aged 15 to 22 and had been killed with a bladed weapon. Whether her death was a ritual sacrifice remains uncertain.

image.caption: The remains of Ballymacombs More Woman were discovered by peat workers in 2023.

sources.originalTitle: Body found in Derry bog decapitated more than 2,000 years ago, coroner finds

segments.body: An inquiry into remains found in a County Derry bog concluded that the Ballymacombs More Woman was between 15 and 22 when she was beheaded from behind more than 2,000 years ago. The investigation, held at the Ulster Museum, used archaeological, forensic and scientific evidence but was not a formal inquest.

segments.title: What the evidence can and cannot say
segments.body: The precise circumstances of her death remain unknown. Evidence suggests it may have been part of a tradition of ritualised killing documented among other Iron Age bodies in north-western Europe, but the inquiry did not establish that as a certainty. Researchers used techniques including micro-CT scanning, digital mapping and 3D imaging; the remains were found without a skull.

content.headline: US loses measles elimination status after more than 5,400 cases in 2026
content.shortHeadline: US loses measles elimination status amid major outbreak
content.standfirst: Health authorities say measles transmission has become endemic again after 26 years of elimination. The designation follows the country’s worst outbreak since 1991, with eight deaths reported in 2026.

sources.originalTitle: US loses measles elimination status amid worst outbreak since 1991

segments.body: The Pan American Health Organization has recognised that measles transmission is once again endemic in the US, which had been measles-free for 26 years. The decision comes after more than 5,400 cases and eight deaths were reported in 2026, the country’s worst outbreak since 1991.

segments.title: A wider vaccination challenge
segments.body: Measles is highly contagious, and about 95% of a community needs to be vaccinated to prevent outbreaks. Experts point to gaps in vaccination coverage and misinformation, while cautioning that the problem predates the current administration and is part of a wider rise in cases. Endemic transmission means people face a continuing risk of infection, rather than cases being typically imported by travellers.

content.headline: US researchers say NIH grant reviews are changing approved studies
content.shortHeadline: Researchers say NIH grant reviews are reshaping approved studies
content.standfirst: An investigation describes researchers being asked to alter funded work, including removing cash payments and references to identity. The NIH says renegotiations are normal and that human experts assess grants; a lawsuit alleging censorship remains unresolved.

image.caption: Researchers describe uncertainty in NIH grant-making over the past two years.

sources.originalTitle: ‘Orwellian’: HIV scientist’s ordeal lays bare Trump officials’ interference in grant-making

segments.body: Researchers told the Guardian that National Institutes of Health officers asked them to change aspects of studies that had passed peer review and been approved for funding. One investigator, Jade Pagkas-Bather, said she removed references to gender identities and racial disparities before receiving a grant, then later replaced planned cash payments to participants with food and transport vouchers.

segments.title: Disputed oversight
segments.body: An analysis by Grant Witness found that the share of continuing NIH grants with changes to titles, abstracts or public-health statements rose from 0.4% in 2023 to 8.6% in 2025 and 8.5% in 2026. The NIH said more than 5,000 new and continuing grants had been renegotiated to support meritorious science and urgent health needs, and that human experts assess them. Pagkas-Bather is among plaintiffs in a lawsuit alleging viewpoint-based discrimination; its outcome is not established.

content.headline: AI-assisted research uncovers a critical flaw in widely used Java software
content.shortHeadline: Researchers find a serious flaw in widely used Java software
content.standfirst: A cybersecurity firm says an AI model helped it find a vulnerability that could allow remote commands to be run through Java’s memory system. Oracle issued a patch, but it is not yet known whether any companies were affected.

sources.originalTitle: Security flaw found in Java, world's third-largest programming language

segments.body: Cybersecurity firm Calif says it used OpenAI’s GPT-6 Cyber, which is not available to the public, to find a flaw in Java memory functions. The vulnerability, which the firm calls Java4Shell, could allow an attacker to run unwanted commands remotely. Java is used across critical sectors, including banking, hospitals, government and telecommunications.

segments.title: Exposure remains unclear
segments.body: Oracle issued a critical patch update that it said included fixes for security vulnerabilities, including this flaw. The BBC reported that it was not yet clear whether any platforms or companies had been affected. Experts cited by the BBC warned that memory vulnerabilities can be serious; the discovery is not evidence that attackers exploited this flaw.

content.headline: Waymo suspends driverless taxi trips on US freeways after California ban
content.shortHeadline: Waymo pulls driverless taxis from US freeways
content.standfirst: Waymo has paused freeway operations nationwide after California barred its vehicles from state freeways over repeated incursions into active construction zones. The company says it is reviewing performance; city-street rides can continue.

sources.originalTitle: Waymo pulls driverless taxis from all US freeways

segments.body: Waymo has temporarily taken its driverless vehicles off all US freeways after California’s Department of Motor Vehicles barred them from the state’s highways. The regulator cited an “imminent hazard to public safety”, including an incident in which several Waymo vehicles entered an active construction zone on US Route 101.

segments.title: What happens next
segments.body: Waymo says it is working with state officials and has temporarily restricted freeway operations in other markets while it evaluates performance. The company said no injuries or collisions were reported in the Route 101 incident; its taxis can still operate on regular city streets. The California restriction will remain until the company demonstrates effective corrective action.

content.headline: Dundee hacker sentenced to six years over phishing and $11.6m thefts
content.shortHeadline: Dundee hacker gets six years for phishing and crypto theft
content.standfirst: Tyler Buchanan admitted taking part in a campaign that targeted technology and telecoms employees with fake login messages, then used stolen credentials and SIM-swapping to steal cryptocurrency. A separate UK case involving a fellow hacking-group member is still proceeding.

image.caption: Tyler Buchanan was arrested in Madrid before being extradited to the United States.

sources.originalTitle: British hacker who stole $11m through text message scheme jailed for six years in US
British hackers face prison for GTA 6 data breach and crypto thefts

segments.body: Tyler Buchanan, 24, from Dundee, has been sentenced to six years in a US federal prison after admitting involvement in a hacking campaign that began in 2021. Prosecutors said Buchanan and co-conspirators used text messages and spoofed work-login pages to steal employees’ credentials, then targeted cryptocurrency investors; authorities calculated losses of more than $11.6m.

segments.title: A separate case involving the same hacking circles
segments.body: TechCrunch reports that Arion Kurtaj, another British member of overlapping hacking groups, has pleaded guilty to attacks including the theft of data from Rockstar Games. He had previously been ordered detained indefinitely after a court found him unable to stand trial, but UK authorities say he will face a public trial. His case is separate from Buchanan’s sentence.

content.headline: US startup opens demonstration plant to make battery graphite from methane
content.shortHeadline: US plant tests a new route to battery-grade graphite
content.standfirst: Molten Industries says its Oakland demonstration plant can produce graphite for battery testing by using electricity to split methane. The company claims a cost advantage, but its output and cost estimates have yet to be proven at commercial scale.

sources.originalTitle: China dominates battery graphite, but this startup could break the monopoly

segments.body: Molten Industries has started operating an Oakland demonstration plant that it says can make battery-grade graphite by heating methane without oxygen, separating it into carbon and hydrogen. The facility is designed to produce about 300 metric tonnes of graphite a year; most of its output will go to unnamed customers testing it in battery cells.

segments.title: A claim awaiting scale-up
segments.body: The company says the process uses three times less electricity than existing methods and that its graphite can match Chinese prices once tariffs are included. China dominates the supply chain, accounting for about three-quarters of graphite anode supply and 97% of synthetic graphite anode production, according to figures cited by TechCrunch. The Oakland plant is a demonstration, not proof that the technology can compete at large scale.

content.headline: E-bike deliveries paused after software bugs drain batteries and disrupt re-ch充
content.shortHeadline: Software bugs halt deliveries of Rivian spinoff’s e-bike
content.standfirst: Also has stopped deliveries of its TM-B e-bike while it prepares a firmware fix for battery drain and charging problems reported by some customers. The delay adds to a difficult launch for a bike built around a software-controlled drive system.

sources.originalTitle: Rivian spinoff Also pauses e-bike deliveries over battery and software bugs

segments.body: Mobility startup Also has paused deliveries of some TM-B Launch Edition e-bikes after identifying software issues, including charging behaviour. Customers have reported batteries losing charge overnight and errors that prevent the bike from recognising a battery; the company says it is working on a firmware update before resuming deliveries.

segments.title: A complex system to fix
segments.body: The TM-B uses a pedal-by-wire design: pedalling drives a generator that replenishes the battery, while a separate motor powers the rear wheel. Also has already faced supply-chain delays and says it will provide another update on the delivery delay by 24 November. The company presents the design as a way to make cycling easier to adopt, but the current problems have delayed customers’ first rides.

content.headline: Nvidia stops shipments of advanced AI chips to China
content.shortHeadline: Nvidia ends H200 chip shipments to China
content.standfirst: Nvidia says it is no longer shipping licensed Hopper data-centre chips to China, despite earlier US approval. The move comes amid new export restrictions and uncertainty about demand, but the company has not explained its decision.

sources.originalTitle: Nvidia isn’t selling any more AI chips to China
Nvidia is abandoning China after Jensen Huang’s ouster

segments.body: Nvidia has stopped shipping its H200 AI chips to China, interim chief executive Colette Kress said on an earnings call. The decision reverses the company’s earlier push to sell the advanced chips there, but Kress did not explain why shipments were ending. The Verge reports that about 600,000 H200 chips were stuck in Hong Kong after Beijing withheld approval for large-scale imports.

segments.title: New restrictions complicate the market
segments.body: The move follows US rules barring advanced chips from foreign data centres that serve Chinese customers remotely.
